tests.claim: Upon arriving on the premises, Ms. Masten witnessed another disabled resident, Marie Ann Thompson ("Ms. Thompson"), being discriminated against by the Defendant in regard to those disabilities. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). Ms. Masten learned from the Defendant's employees that Ms. Thompson was not wanted on the property because of her disabilities, and that the Defendant essentially planned to evict her. Ms. Masten began assisting Ms. Thompson in drafting and filing a charge with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission ("OCRC") against the Defendant for violations of Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02(H)(12) and 42 U.S.C. § 3617. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). After assisting Ms. Thompson with her OCRC filing, and after K&D Managers learned of Ms. Masten assisting Ms. Thompsan with the OCRC charge, the Defendant began discriminating against Ms. Masten in various ways. tests.claim: Upon arriving on the premises, Ms. Masten witnessed another disabled resident, Marie Ann Thompson ("Ms. Thompson"), being discriminated against by the Defendant in regard to those disabilities. Ms. Masten learned from the Defendant's employees that Ms. Thompson was not wanted on the property because of her disabilities, and that the Defendant essentially planned to evict her. (Def.'s Answer & Counterclaim at P 10). Ms. Masten began assisting Ms. Thompson in drafting and filing a charge with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission ("OCRC") against the Defendant for violations of Ohio Revised Code § 4112.02(H)(12) and 42 U.S.C. § 3617. elements.explanation: The brief identifies dated activity by Masten: helping another tenant file an OCRC discrimination charge around October 15, 2010, filing her own OCRC charge in November 2010, and trying unsuccessfully to withdraw it by July 11, 2011. But it pleads those acts as Fair Housing/OCRC activity, not as an R.C. 5321.02 protected act such as a code-enforcement complaint, landlord complaint, or tenant-organization activity.
elements.quote: On or about October 15, 2010 Masten assisted another tenant of the premises in filing a charge of discrimination against K&D with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission. Masten subsequently filed her own charge of discrimination against K&D with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission.

elements.label: The landlord knew of the protected activity
elements.requirement: The brief says how the landlord came to know of it.
elements.explanation: The brief says K&D learned of Masten's assistance and knew of her own OCRC charge, but it does not explain how K&D came to know except by noting that K&D later asked whether she would drop the charge. The cited/quoted material supports knowledge in general, but not the mechanism of knowledge required by the element.
elements.quote: After assisting Ms. Thompson with her OCRC filing, and after K&D Managers learned of Ms. Masten assisting Ms. Thompsan with the OCRC charge, the Defendant began discriminating against Ms. Masten in various ways. ... In February of 2011, the Defendant inquired whether Ms. Masten would consider dropping her own charge with the Ohio Civil Rights Commission.

elements.label: The landlord took one of the acts the statute forbids
elements.requirement: The brief names the act -- the eviction, the rent increase, the reduced service.
elements.explanation: The brief names the alleged retaliatory acts: the 81-day notice of nonrenewal and the later eviction/forcible-entry action. The brief’s quoted trial-court entry and citations state that K&D served the notice, served a three-day notice to vacate, and filed the eviction complaint.
elements.quote: On July 12, 2011, after K&D Management discovered that Ms. Masten was unsuccessful in dropping her OCRC charge, K&D Management retaliated against Ms. Masten by issuing an eighty-one (81) dav notice of non-renewal of lease, requiring her to leave the property on September 30, 2011. ... Subsequently, K&D Management brought an eviction action in order to coerce, intimidate, threaten, and penalize her for filing complaints with the OCRC when Ms. Masten became a holdover tenant.

elements.label: The connection between the two is pleaded
elements.requirement: The brief says why the act followed the protected activity -- normally the timing, and anything the landlord said.
elements.explanation: The brief pleads causation through timing and motive: K&D allegedly acted after learning of the OCRC activity and issued nonrenewal the day after Masten learned she could not withdraw her OCRC complaint. Support is partial because the brief cites an OCRC probable-cause determination and timing, but the supplied text does not include underlying record excerpts or landlord statements directly proving the causal link.
elements.quote: The Ms. Masten received the notice that her lease would not be renewed on July 12, 2011, the day after she discovered that she would be unable to withdraw her OCRC complaint (Id. at Exhibit B, pg. 3). The landlord's actions occurred following the "exercise of protected activity" and supported the Commission's determination that illegal retaliation had occurred.

III. LAW AND ARGUMENT
A. Motion for Summary Judgment Standard
The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." No genuine issue of material fact exists when "it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgement is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party. Temple o. Wean United, Inc., 50 Ohio St.2d 317, 327, 364 N.E.2d 267 (1977). Summary judgment proceedings under the Civil Rules are applicable to forcible entry and detainer actions. Siegler v. To prevail on a motion for summary judgment, the moving party bears the initial burden of identifying those portions of the record that demonstrate the absence of genuine issues of material fact concerning an essential element of the nonmoving party's claim. Dresher v. Burt, 75 Ohio St.3d 280, 292, 662 N.E.2d 264 (1996). When the moving party properly supports its motion for summary judgment, the nonmoving party may not rest upon the mere allegation of the pleadings, but must set forth specific facts demonstrating that there is a genuine issue for trial. Jackson v. Alert Fire and Safety Equip., Inc., 58 Ohio St.3d 48, 51-52, 567 N.E.2d 1027 (1991). If the party does not so respond, then summary judgment shall be entered against that party. Id.

MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT
I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
This Court should grant plaintiff's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the first claim for possession in plaintiff's Complaint because there is no genuine issue of material fact. The Estate is entitled to possession of the Premises pursuant to an order of the Geauga County Probate Court, and because defendants signed a deed to the Premises over to the Estate pursuant to that court order. When defendants did not vacate the Premises, plaintiff notified defendants to leave the Premises in accordance with the requirements under R.C. § 1923.04(A) before bringing a forcible entry and detainer action. Therefore, the Estate is entitled to possession of the Premises and this Court should grant plaintiff's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on plaintiff's possession claim.

§1923.04(A) requires that before commencing an action for forcible entry and detain, the party seeking possession of a premises must:
notify the adverse party to leave the premises ... three or more days before beginning the action, by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by handing a written copy of the notice to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises from which the defendant is sought to be evicted.
The notice itself shall contain the following language in a clearly visible manner: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Id. The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." No genuine issue of material fact exists when "it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgement is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party. I. PRELIMINARY STATEMENT
This Court should grant plaintiff's Motion for Partial Summary Judgment on the first claim for possession in plaintiff's Complaint because there is no genuine issue of material fact. The Estate is entitled to possession of the Premises pursuant to an order of the Geauga County Probate Court, and because defendants signed a deed to the Premises over to the Estate pursuant to that court order. A. Motion for Summary Judgment Standard
The Ohio Rules of Civil Procedure provide under Civ.R 56(C) that summary judgment is proper if "the pleadings, depositions, answers to interrogatories, written admissions, affidavits, transcripts of evidence, and written stipulations of fact, if any ... show that there is no genuine issue as to any material fact and that the moving party is entitled to judgment as a matter of law." No genuine issue of material fact exists when "it appears from the evidence that reasonable minds can come to but one conclusion, and viewing such evidence most strongly in favor of the party against whom the motion for summary judgement is made, that conclusion is adverse to that party. Temple o. Wean United, Inc., 50 Ohio St.2d 317, 327, 364 N.E.2d 267 (1977). Summary judgment proceedings under the Civil Rules are applicable to forcible entry and detainer actions. Siegler v. notify the adverse party to leave the premises ... three or more days before beginning the action, by certified mail, return receipt requested, or by handing a written copy of the notice to the defendant in person, or by leaving it at the defendant's usual place of abode or at the premises from which the defendant is sought to be evicted.
The notice itself shall contain the following language in a clearly visible manner: "You are being asked to leave the premises. If you do not leave, an eviction action may be initiated against you. If you are in doubt regarding your legal rights and obligations as a tenant, it is recommended that you seek legal assistance." Id. rule_audit.summary: A forcible entry and detainer action requires that the party seeking possession first serve a notice to leave the premises, in the statutory form and by a permitted method, and then wait the statutory period before filing.
